Sintay 23-00079 BSCS Research Title: A Risk-Based Two-Factor Student Verification and Event Attendance Management System Using Near Field Communication (NFC), Personal Identification Number (PIN) Authentication, and Quick Response (QR) Credential Validation Rationale: As the population in universities continues to increase, student verification and attendance monitoring during events become more complex and difficult to manage using traditional methods. Many institutions still rely on manual processes such as visual inspection of identification cards and paper-based attendance systems, which are prone to human error, inefficiency, and security risks. Unauthorized individuals may gain access to the institution by using borrowed or outdated IDs, while attendance records may become inaccurate due to proxy attendance. While single-factor automated systems, such as those relying solely on Near Field Communication (NFC), offer improvements in speed, they present critical security vulnerabilities. Possession of a physical NFC credential alone does not guarantee the identity of the user, as NFC UIDs can be easily borrowed, cloned, or misused. Furthermore, relying heavily

To address these vulnerabilities, there is a necessity to transition from outdated, single-factor identification toward a modernized, multi-layered authentication framework. This study proposes the design and development of a risk-based two-factor authentication system that combines NFC technology (as a possession factor) with Personal Identification Number (PIN) authentication (as a knowledge factor). To specifically counter the threat of credential cloning, the system introduces QR credential validation to cross-check the physical printed ID against the NFC-linked database record. By implementing adaptive, risk-based verification modes (Fast, Standard, and High-Security), the system dynamically scales security requirements based on the transaction's context, maintaining high throughput for routine entry while enforcing strict validation for restricted events or suspicious activities. Ultimately, this system shifts the security paradigm from manual, transaction-by-transaction approval to an automated, alert-driven monitoring approach, providing a faster, more secure, and data-driven solution for modern campus environments. normalized: 11 TAGUIG CITY UNIVERSITY ABSTRACT Campus student verification and event attendance require reliable credential checks and traceable records. Paper-based attendance and reliance on a single credential can leave identity verification separate from recordkeeping. This study addressed the need to combine configurable credential validation, attendance recording, and monitoring within one workflow. A quantitative developmental and descriptive-evaluative design produced a WinUI 3 prototype integrating an ESP32 and PN532 NFC reader, PIN authentication, camera-based QR validation, local MySQL storage, and Firebase Firestore synchronization. Operators selected Fast, Standard, or High-Security modes, with QR providing an additional credential-integrity check. Evaluation included 80 proposed-system survey respondents, 70 separate manual-process student respondents, and controlled observation of 70 participants completing 210 successful entry trials across three modes. Mean internal latency was 11.49, 57.37, and 54.06 milliseconds for Fast, Standard, and High-Security modes; recorded Standard PIN and High-Security PIN/QR interaction averaged 2.505 and 5.799 seconds. Observed credential-decision accuracy was 100% (222/222) under researcher-labelled controlled conditions, while overall proposed-system survey means were 3.74 for students, 3.63 for security personnel, and 3.81 for administrative respondents, all Highly Satisfactory. Proposed-system student ratings exceeded manual-process ratings (3.742 versus 2.284), Welch t(89.08) = 15.12, p < .001; however, differing timing boundaries prevented a matched complete-task speed comparison.

normalized: 18 TAGUIG CITY UNIVERSITY CHAPTER 1 THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND Project Context As educational institutions adapt to the digital era, traditional manual campus management (relying on visual ID card checks at entry gates and paper-based sign-in sheets at events) has proven inefficient, error-prone, and insecure. Visual inspection allows borrowed, lost, or outdated IDs to pass unverified, while paper sign-ins create severe queue bottlenecks, invite proxy attendance, and fail to enforce real-time restricted event lists. Automated identification systems have been shown to improve verification accuracy and reduce manual processing errors (Rashid, 2024), and while automated single-factor systems (such as standalone NFC or RFID) improve entry speed, they introduce significant security vulnerabilities. Possession of a physical NFC credential alone does not guarantee the holder's true identity, as NFC UIDs can be easily borrowed, shared, or cloned (El Gaabouri et al., 2023; Mohammed et al., 2023). Furthermore, relying on security personnel to manually validate every individual digital transaction creates operational bottlenecks during high-traffic periods and conflicts with their primary responsibility of enforcing physical security. To address these vulnerabilities, this study develops a prototype for a Risk-Based Two-Factor Student Verification and Event Attendance Management System. The architecture integrates Near Field Communication (NFC) as a primary possession factor, Personal Identification Number (PIN) authentication as a knowledge factor, and Quick Response (QR) credential validation as a credential integrity validation to cross-check physical IDs against

The system also incorporates a decentralized, student-facing web portal for out-of-band email OTP PIN resets, ensuring autonomous credential recovery without burdening administrators. To balance security with operational efficiency, the system applies dynamic verification modes configurable by security personnel, event organizers, or administrators: Fast Mode (NFC only) for low-risk, high-throughput routine entry; Standard Mode (NFC + PIN) for routine identity assurance; and High-Security Mode (NFC + PIN + QR) for restricted events. Purpose and Description The purpose of this study is to design and develop a risk-based, two-factor verification system prototype that strengthens campus security and identity verification processes through Near Field Communication (NFC) technology, Personal Identification Number (PIN) authentication, and QR credential validation. By replacing single-factor identification methods, the proposed system aims to provide a faster, more secure, and data-driven approach to validating individuals entering university facilities, particularly by preventing unauthorized access through borrowed, lost, or cloned credentials.

Although consecutive failed attempts are limited through the system's lockout mechanism, resistance to sophisticated attacks is beyond the scope of the prototype. Static QR codes may also be copied or photographed. If both an NFC credential and its corresponding QR code are duplicated, the system relies on PIN authentication as the remaining knowledge-based safeguard. ● Functional Exclusions: The prototype evaluation focuses on functional performance, software quality, verification accuracy, security effectiveness, and user acceptance. It does not include full campus surveillance, visitor management, payment processing, or long-term hardware durability testing. ● Testing Demographics: The prototype testing and user evaluation phase is limited to students within the College of Information and Communication Technology (CICT) using purposive and convenience sampling. Calo et al. (2021) introduced a hybrid identification and visual verification model, establishing an early local precedent for layered authentication. Pantilon (2025) and Bergosa et al. (2024) confirmed the usability and effectiveness of QR-coded identification in local attendance monitoring contexts. Valdez et al. (2024) and Velasco (2023) demonstrated that RFID and NFC-based systems can be successfully implemented for campus access monitoring in Philippine universities. Bolasco et al. (2025) further highlighted the administrative value of automated attendance in local institutional settings. However, across these studies, existing local implementations focus primarily on single-technology solutions like QR only, RFID only, or NFC only which do not address the security risks associated with single-factor identification, such as credential borrowing, cloning, or unauthorized sharing. Despite the advancements presented in both foreign and local studies, a clear gap remains in the existing literature. While foreign literature demonstrates the vulnerability of single-factor NFC authentication and proposes multi-factor and risk-based frameworks as solutions, no local study has implemented a two-factor NFC and PIN authentication system for campus access control and event attendance management. Additionally, no local study has integrated QR credential validation as an anti-cloning integrity check within a campus verification system, nor has any local study applied a risk-based mode selection framework distinguishing between Fast Mode, Standard Mode, and High-Security Mode to adaptively balance security and usability in high-traffic academic environments.

The student then taps an NFC-enabled identification card on the PN532 reader, after which the ESP32 reads the card's Unique Identifier (UID). The system retrieves the corresponding student record and validates the NFC UID. If no matching student is found, the system displays an "Unauthorized" result. If a valid student record is found, the system checks the student's enrollment status. Students marked as Not Active or Expelled are denied access. For restricted events, the system also checks whether the student is registered for the selected event. Students who are not registered are denied access. After the eligibility checks, the system applies the verification mode based on the determined risk level. Fast Mode uses NFC authentication only. Standard Mode requires the student to enter their PIN, which the system validates automatically. High-Security Mode requires both PIN authentication and QR credential validation. The QR code is scanned using the camera and cross-checked against the NFC-linked student record to detect credential mismatches or possible NFC cloning. Failed PIN or QR validation results in access denial, with the transaction logged for security monitoring. If verification is successful, the system records the student's attendance with a timestamp, updates the entry/exit state, and records the successful transaction. For the Student Verification / Entry-Exit process, the user opens the Student Verification / Entrance-Exit screen. The system first determines the appropriate risk level for verification and then scans the student's NFC-enabled identification card. The ESP32 reads the UID and transmits it for validation. The system retrieves and validates the student's record and checks the enrollment status. If no valid record is found, the system displays an "Unauthorized" result.

At the edge layer, a student taps their NFC-enabled ID on the ESP32-based reader with PN532, which extracts the UID and transmits it to the backend server over the local network using a USB cable. The backend then validates the UID, checks the student's enrollment status, and for restricted events it confirms event registration. Based on this assessment, the system determines the required verification mode: Fast Mode for low-risk transactions, Standard Mode for medium-risk, or High-Security Mode for high-risk transactions. The student's information and assigned mode are displayed on the monitoring interface for visibility only; no manual decision is taken at this stage. The system then authenticates automatically according to the assigned mode. Fast Mode requires no further input. Standard Mode prompts the student for their PIN. High-Security Mode requires both PIN entry and a QR code scan, cross-checked against the NFC-linked record to detect cloning or mismatch. The system also performs an anti-tailgating check based on the credential's entry/exit state. If all required factors pass, access is granted, the entry/exit state is updated, and the transaction is logged. If any factor fails, access is denied, the attempt is logged, and a security alert is generated. Alerts are triggered by specific conditions of three consecutive failed PIN attempts, QR mismatches, Inactive/Expelled access attempts, unregistered restricted-event attempts, or

Students then tap their NFC-enabled IDs on the ESP32-based attendance station with PN532 reader, which captures the UID and timestamp before transmitting the data to the backend server over the local network via USB cable. The backend validates the UID, verifies the student's enrollment status, confirms registration for the active event, and determines the appropriate verification mode based on the event configuration and any detected real-time risk flags. The student's information and assigned verification mode are displayed for system tracking only; attendance decisions are made automatically by the system rather than manually by an administrator. Authentication is then performed according to the assigned verification mode. Fast Mode requires only the NFC credential, Standard Mode requires NFC and PIN authentication, while High-Security Mode requires NFC, PIN, and QR credential validation. The system also performs an anti-tailgating check using the credential's attendance state. If all required checks pass, attendance is recorded, the attendance state is updated, and the transaction is logged. If any required authentication factor fails, attendance is denied, the failed attempt is logged, and a security alert is generated.

It outlines the system's operational performance, presents the functional testing results, and discusses the performance metrics and survey evaluations gathered from students, security personnel, faculty members, event organizers, and administrators. 4.1 Prototype Implementation Summary The prototype combines NFC credential capture with a C# WinUI 3 application for student verification and event-attendance management. An ESP32 microcontroller and PN532 NFC reader provide NFC capture through a USB serial connection to the computer. PIN entry and camera-based QR scanning are handled by the application. Fast mode requires NFC validation, Standard mode adds PIN authentication, and High-Security mode adds QR credential validation. Verification requirements are selected through the configured operating mode rather than an automatically calculated individual risk score. The application uses local MySQL storage and Firebase Firestore synchronization to support its record-management workflow. Its interfaces present verification decisions, student information, transaction records, and security alerts. Relevant program code is included in Appendix E, while the documented functionality test cases and results are presented in Appendix H.

These findings address SOP 6C through comparison of student-reported evaluations. They do not establish a causal improvement attributable solely to the attendance method because the groups consisted of different respondents and the questionnaires used process-specific wording. The timing and rate findings for SOP 6A and SOP 6B remain descriptive component measurements rather than a matched complete-task comparison. 4.3.5.4 Supplementary Validation-Procedure Comparison The manual simulation collected attendance information without checking identification cards or enrollment status. This represents the absence of a validation step in the simulated procedure, not evidence that participants were unenrolled or that their attendance records were fraudulent.

Responses were scored as 4 for Strongly Agree, 3 for Agree, 2 for Disagree, and 1 for Strongly Disagree. For each item, the weighted mean was calculated as (4f4 + 3f3 + 2f2 + f1) / N. All 111 item-frequency totals and weighted scores were reconciled with the supplied survey worksheet. Category means were calculated from unrounded item means. The overall result for each respondent group was calculated as the arithmetic mean of its category means, giving equal weight to each category. This convention matters because the number of items differs across categories. Final values were rounded to two decimal places only after calculation. The group results were not pooled into a single overall system score because the role-specific instruments cover different indicators and category sets.

Internal latency averaged 11.49, 57.37, and 54.06 ms for Fast, Standard, and High-Security. Recorded interaction averaged 2.505 seconds in Standard and 5.799 seconds in High-Security. Researcher-labelled applicable credential decisions yielded observed accuracy of 100.00% (222/222), while the overall recorded denial proportion was 4.11% (18/438). Two deliberately triggered lockouts among 152 captured PIN submissions yielded a recorded lockout rate of 1.32%. These are controlled recorded-sample findings, not universal accuracy or ordinary-user failure estimates. The manual paper-attendance baseline contained 70 writing observations with mean duration of 21.803 seconds and sample SD of 4.436 seconds. The timed manual procedure contained no ID or enrollment validation. System-evaluation means were 3.74 for students, 3.63 for security personnel, and 3.81 for faculty, event-organizer, and administrative respondents, all interpreted as Highly Satisfactory. The manual pre-evaluation mean was 2.28, interpreted as Unsatisfactory. The overall survey comparison was statistically significant, t(89.08) = 15.12, p < .001, with a 1.458-point mean difference favoring the proposed system. Together, the observations and surveys document the prototype's measured component performance, tested rule enforcement, and favorable perceived quality. A matched end-to-end performance comparison and independent error or fraud audit remain necessary to establish complete-task speed improvement and comparative incident rates.

Summary of Findings Prototype Implementation and Functionality The prototype integrated an ESP32 microcontroller and PN532 NFC reader with a C# WinUI 3 application. The serial-connected reader supplied NFC credential information, while the application handled PIN entry, camera-based QR validation, configured access decisions, transaction records, and monitoring interfaces. Local MySQL storage and Firebase Firestore synchronization supported the record-management workflow. Fast mode used NFC validation, Standard mode added PIN authentication, and High-Security mode added QR credential validation. Mode selection was configured by an authorized operator rather than automatically determined from an individual risk score. QR matching functioned as an additional credential-integrity check, not an independently established third authentication factor. Appendix H documented 16 functionality cases, all marked PASS. Interpretation of Results The role-specific evaluations indicated favorable perceived quality of the proposed prototype. Students gave their highest category rating to Functional Suitability at 3.76. Security personnel also rated Functional Suitability highest at 3.84, while their lowest category rating was Performance Efficiency at 3.45. The faculty/event-organizer/administrator group rated Portability highest at 3.92 and Performance Efficiency lowest at 3.68. These within-group patterns help identify strengths and priorities without creating an unsupported pooled ranking across different instruments. The manual group reported less favorable perceptions in four of the five categories. Usability, at 2.64, remained Satisfactory, while Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Security were Unsatisfactory. The overall-score t-test supported a statistically significant difference between the manual and proposed-system groups' reported evaluations. However, group differences and method-specific item wording limited attribution of that difference solely to the attendance method. The observation data showed internal processing on a millisecond scale and recorded PIN/QR interaction on a seconds scale. Fast had the shortest internal latency and within-round entry spacing. Standard's mean internal latency exceeded High-Security's, so the internal data did not show a simple increase with each additional credential stage. The fixed mode order also limited causal interpretation of the lower mean PIN duration recorded in High-Security mode.

Distinguish logical state-rule tests from observation of physical gate bypass or tailgating. Report expected and actual outcomes for each applicable attempt rather than inferring security effectiveness from survey agreement alone. e. Expand Offline, Synchronization, and Recovery Testing. Test prolonged disconnections, stale student-status data, simultaneous offline terminals, conflicting updates, interrupted synchronization, and recovery after

The documented functionality cases and observation records demonstrated the expected responses under the tested conditions. The three proposed-system respondent groups gave favorable overall evaluations, while the independent student survey comparison showed significantly higher reported ratings for the proposed system than for the manual process. The recorded component timings, security-condition outcomes, and manual writing baseline provided useful descriptive findings. However, their different timing boundaries did not establish a matched complete-task speed or throughput advantage. The controlled tests and survey ratings also did not establish universal security effectiveness, automatic individual risk scoring, or readiness for immediate institution-wide deployment. The findings therefore supported the prototype's demonstrated functionality and perceived acceptability within the evaluation setting. Further matched performance measurement, broader respondent evaluation, direct security and recovery testing, and operational assessment are needed before making stronger claims about full-scale institutional effectiveness.
